strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear desiderata (D1-D3) addressing real limitations of prior batch selection methods

Solid theoretical foundation: nuclear norm connection to optimization utility and intra-sample diversity is mathematically sound, with empirical validation (Figure 2) showing strong correlation (ρ≈0.6-0.8)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 4 datasets and 2 models with consistent improvements (2-5% gains) over SOTA baseline GREATS and thoughtful ablation studies demonstrating necessity of both components

Novel application of nuclear norm to batch selection and clever Kronecker factorization (Theorem 3.2) for efficient Johnson-Lindenstrauss projection avoiding explicit storage of large projection matrices
Achieves training speedup over full-dataset fine-tuning (3.41 vs 2.27 samples/s on MMLU) while improving generalization, addressing practical efficiency concerns
Honest discussion of limitations (SVD overhead, scalability to larger models) and comprehensive appendix with proofs, hyperparameter analysis, and experimental details
weaknesses: Modest empirical improvements (~5% over GREATS on Qwen-2.5-7B MMLU) with substantial variance (error bars ±0.36) raise questions about practical significance; no statistical significance testing provided

Claims of 'no external resources' are misleading: requires dataset-specific tuning of trade-off parameter α (sensitive inverted-U in Figure 7, varies 1.5×10⁻³-7×10⁻³ across tasks) and selection ratios (12.5%-50% in Table 5 with no principled guidance)

SVD computational overhead for nuclear norm not fully characterized; paper admits overhead 'may introduce non-negligible overhead' (Appendix E) but provides no wall-clock measurements; randomized SVD abandoned due to precision loss without quantitative comparison

Intra-sample diversity connection is indirect and insufficiently validated: no empirical verification that language model logits actually achieve the rank-theoretic bounds in Lemma 3.1; simplified Figure 3 illustration lacks real examples showing rank-diversity correlation

Optimization utility approximation (Eq. 8) assumes ⟨∆(x), δL(x)⟩ dominates; but correlation variance in Figure 2 (ρ ranges 0.2-0.9) indicates significant approximation failures; no analysis of when assumption breaks down, especially early in training

Scalability concerns: only 7-8B models tested; paper defers larger models and long sequences to future work; batch size B=8 is unrealistically small; efficiency still 2.7× slower than random selection (3.41 vs 9.29 samples/s)

Inter-sample diversity measure lacks justification: simple Euclidean distance in projected space chosen without comparison to alternatives (cosine similarity, learned metrics); FIFO buffer may not capture representative samples

Unfair baseline comparisons: RHO-Loss uses suboptimal Llama-2-13B surrogate reference model (acknowledged but unaddressed); GREATS validation set specifications unclear; no comparison with recent methods like LESS

Limited experimental scope: only instruction-tuning tasks (MMLU, ScienceQA, GSM8K, HumanEval); general pretraining or domain adaptation scenarios untested; no analysis of which samples selected or selection evolution during training

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear desiderata (D1-D3) and systematic baseline comparison
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 4 benchmarks and 2 models with consistent improvements
Avoids external dependencies (reference models, validation sets) in principle
Includes proper ablation studies (Table 4) showing both components contribute meaningfully
Provides theoretical grounding through matrix norm relationships and Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma
Achieves practical efficiency gains: better accuracy than full-dataset training with comparable throughput
weaknesses: Nuclear norm justification is weak: Figure 2 shows moderate (0.2-0.8) and highly variable correlations, not the 'strong correlation' claimed. The connection between nuclear norm and loss reduction lacks rigor.

Extensive per-dataset hyperparameter tuning contradicts 'general' and 'external resource-free' claims: selection ratios vary 12.5%-50% (Table 5), and α requires dataset-specific tuning (Table 6, ranging 1e-3 to 7e-3).

SVD computational overhead inadequately addressed: for N×V matrices with large V (~150k for Qwen), SVD complexity O(NV·min(N,V)) is non-negligible but dismissed in Appendix E without cost analysis or comparison to simpler alternatives.
Statistical significance not established: multiple improvements fall within 1-2 standard deviations (e.g., Llama MMLU: 40.16±0.58 vs GREATS 39.04±0.29), and no significance tests performed.

Baseline fairness concerns: RHO-Loss uses weaker reference model (Llama-2-13B vs 70B for computational reasons), MaxGrad shows suspicious slowness (0.29-0.98 throughput), GREATS validation set very small (5 samples).
Insufficient diversity-utility analysis: simple linear combination (Eq. 11) with per-dataset α tuning; no investigation of which samples are filtered or why performance degrades at K>4 (Figure 4).

Weak empirical validation of core mechanism: Figure 3 shows toy examples but no validation that nuclear norm captures real semantic diversity; no comparison with entropy-based or other diversity measures.
Missing experimental details: memory buffer size M not specified in main experiments; SVD implementation (full vs approximate) unclear; early training behavior before buffer fills unaddressed.

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear desiderata (D1-D3) and systematic comparison of existing methods
Principled theoretical foundation combining nuclear norm with first-order optimization analysis and rank-based diversity interpretation (Lemma 3.1)
Clever computational design using bilinear factorization (Theorem 3.2) reducing complexity from O(NVd) to O((N+V)d log(NV)) while preserving Johnson-Lindenstrauss guarantees
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across four benchmarks and two model sizes with proper baselines, ablations, and sensitivity analysis
Consistent SOTA results outperforming GREATS across all benchmarks (e.g., Qwen-2.5-7B MMLU: 63.34% vs 58.19%)
Successfully achieves all three design goals: no external resources, no validation set, no reference model
Clear presentation with intuitive explanations and helpful visualizations
weaknesses: SVD computation overhead for nuclear norm calculation inadequately addressed—acknowledged as 'non-negligible' for long sequences but not thoroughly investigated; approximate methods reportedly degrade performance without quantification
Efficiency gains are more modest than claimed—18-23% throughput improvements on some benchmarks, and UDS slower than full dataset in some cases; wall-clock time analysis missing

Requires substantial dataset-specific tuning: selection ratios vary dramatically across datasets (Qwen-2.5-7B uses 12.5%-50%) and optimal α values vary 3-4x (Table 6), undermining 'practical' and 'automatic' claims
Theoretical justification for optimization utility relies on first-order Taylor approximation with no convergence analysis; Figure 2 shows noisy correlation without rigorous guarantees
Nuclear norm serves as proxy for both utility and diversity—conflates distinct concepts; a sample could be high-utility but low-diversity (repetitive but challenging)
Limited scope: only evaluates supervised fine-tuning with LoRA (rank=8) and batch size 8; scalability to full fine-tuning and larger batches unclear
Missing ablations on distance metric choice, memory buffer strategies, and systematic analysis of failure modes
Code unavailable (blank in abstract); reproducibility would benefit from provided implementation
Comparison with GREATS may be unfair—GREATS requires validation set while UDS requires α/ratio tuning, different types of external knowledge
Modest practical impact: accuracy improvements of 3-7% over GREATS are meaningful but not transformative; efficiency gains limited

strengths: Clear problem formulation with three well-motivated desiderata (D1-D3) that systematically address limitations of prior work

Solid mathematical foundation using nuclear norm with Lemma 3.1 establishing meaningful bounds between Frobenius and nuclear norms; empirical correlations strongly support claims (Figures 2-3 show ~0.8+ Spearman correlations)
Elegant technical design using bilinear random projections (Theorem 3.2) reducing complexity from O(NVd) to O((N+V)d log(NV)), avoiding explicit storage of ~74GB projection matrices

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 4 diverse domains, 2 models, consistent improvements over GREATS (e.g., +5.15% on MMLU), maintained/improved efficiency, thorough ablations, additional experiments on long contexts and OOD robustness

Both components (nuclear norm and diversity distance) proven necessary through ablations; full fine-tuning experiments (Appendix B.3) and instruction-tuned models (Appendix B.3) demonstrate generalization
Honest discussion of limitations (SVD overhead, lack of rigorous proofs) and comprehensive appendix with implementation details supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: SVD computational overhead contradicts efficiency claims: paper claims 'no computational overhead' but acknowledges in Appendix E that SVD 'may introduce non-negligible overhead'; attempted randomized SVD degraded performance, unresolved tension between efficiency and accuracy

Theory-practice gaps: first-order Taylor expansion (Eqs. 5-8) assumes small logits changes; intra-sample diversity connection is intuitive rather than rigorous—no formal proof that rank(L) correlates with prediction diversity; Figures 2-3 show ~0.2-0.4 scatter indicating probabilistic relationship

Significant hyperparameter sensitivity undermines generality: α varies 5x across datasets (Table 6: 1.5-7×10⁻³); selection ratios vary 4x (Table 5: 12.5%-50%); sensitivity curves (Figures 6-8) show dataset-dependent saturation points

Modest empirical improvements over SOTA in several cases: ScienceQA +1.02% (95.19% vs 94.17%), GSM8K +1.30% are within or near error bars; only MMLU shows substantial gains (+5.15%); statistical significance testing absent despite reported error margins

Limited algorithmic novelty: nuclear norm and SRFT are established techniques; combining utility with diversity in selection is standard practice; contribution is primarily empirical application and engineering rather than novel insights

Unresolved theoretical limitations acknowledged but not addressed: authors unable to provide rigorous proof for nuclear norm-loss reduction correlation or effective matrix rank relationship; no convergence guarantees or sample complexity analysis

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (MMLU, ScienceQA, GSM8K, HumanEval) and models with detailed ablations and sensitivity analyses
Technically sound methodology for inter-sample diversity using SRFT-based random projection with rigorous Johnson-Lindenstrauss theoretical guarantees
Thorough empirical analysis with reproducible implementation, clear algorithmic description, and honest acknowledgment of limitations
Consistent (if modest) improvements across multiple benchmarks and configurations
Well-structured paper with clear motivation and good use of figures for illustration
weaknesses: Core technical contribution lacks rigorous theoretical justification: nuclear norm's correlation with loss reduction is only empirically demonstrated on limited settings (Figure 2 shows Spearman correlation ~0.8, not perfect; proof explicitly acknowledged as missing in Appendix E)
SVD computational cost of N×V logits matrices (up to 512×152k for Qwen-2.5-7B) not adequately accounted in 'faster than full-dataset' claims; throughput improvements are modest (9-32%)

Method requires per-dataset hyperparameter tuning: selection fraction K varies from 12.5% to 50% (Table 5), and α varies by order of magnitude (1×10^-3 to 7×10^-3, Table 6), undermining 'no external resources' claims—this is a form of validation overhead

Improvements over prior SOTA (GREATS) are modest on most benchmarks: MMLU +5.15%, but ScienceQA +1.02%, GSM8K +1.30%, HumanEval +1.24%, with overlapping error bars on several tasks questioning statistical significance
First-order Taylor expansion (Eq. 5-8) makes informal assumptions about scale-insensitivity of gradients that aren't universally valid; validity conditions not discussed
Intra-sample diversity claim conflates matrix rank with semantic diversity—connection between more varied singular values and better training samples is assumed rather than rigorously justified
Limited experimental scope: only 7-8B models tested; only 5 datasets; correlations (Figures 2-3) shown only on MMLU; ablations (Table 4) only on Qwen-2.5-7B
Unfair comparison due to different selection fractions K across methods, making it unclear whether improvements come from better selection or simply using less data

strengths: Well-motivated problem with three clear desiderata (D1-D3) addressing genuine limitations of existing online batch selection methods
Novel use of nuclear norm to jointly capture optimization utility and intra-sample diversity, with strong empirical validation (Spearman correlation >0.8 in Figures 2-3)

Efficient technical design avoiding external resources: logits-based scoring without gradient computation, clever structured bilinear projection (Theorem 3.2) reducing storage from ~74GB to ~1.2GB with Johnson-Lindenstrauss guarantees

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 4 benchmarks, 2 models, consistent improvements (+5.15% on MMLU vs GREATS, faster than full-dataset training), extensive ablations and sensitivity analyses across diverse settings (Table 10-14)
Practical applicability: no requirement for reference models or validation sets, plug-and-play integration with SFT pipeline, LoRA-compatible
Reproducibility: clear pseudocode (Algorithm 1), detailed hyperparameters and experimental configuration, honest limitations discussion
weaknesses: Theoretical foundation relies entirely on first-order Taylor approximation (Eq. 5-8) without analysis of approximation validity across training phases; rank-diversity relationship in Figure 3 shows correlation but lacks rigorous causal proof

SVD computation overhead acknowledged but unresolved: randomized SVD rejected for 'loss in precision' without quantitative analysis; no breakdown of SVD time as percentage of total training time, raising scalability concerns for long sequences and large models

Hyperparameter tuning significantly reduces practical applicability: trade-off factor α varies 1-7×10⁻³ across datasets/models without principled selection method; data selection fractions vary 12.5%-50%, making it unclear if improvements stem from the algorithm or dataset-specific tuning

Experimental design concerns: non-uniform data selection fractions (Table 5) may confound results; RHO-Loss uses suboptimal surrogate reference model; GREATS penalized for requiring validation set despite being designed for it; LoRA-only primary experiments may not generalize to full fine-tuning

Limited generalization analysis: all tasks are instruction-following QA; method shows notably smaller improvements on instruction-tuned models (2.2% vs 5.15% on base models); scalability to 70B+ models undemonstrated; no exploration of failure modes or edge cases
FIFO buffer strategy not critical (ablation Table 7 shows equivalence to alternatives); buffer size M=1024 appears 4× larger than saturation point (~256), suggesting suboptimal design choices

Statistical rigor: no significance testing performed; some improvements marginal with overlapping error bars; nuclear norm vs. cheaper alternatives (Frobenius norm, top-k singular values) not compared
